content: 1. Azithromycin has been associated with rare but serious allergic reactions, including angioedema, anaphylaxis, and severe dermatologic conditions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Fatalities have been reported in some cases. Even after initial successful symptomatic treatment, allergic symptoms have been known to recur after discontinuation of symptomatic therapy, even without further exposure to azithromycin. These patients may require prolonged observation and symptomatic management. The relationship between these episodes and the long tissue half-life of azithromycin, leading to prolonged antigen exposure, is currently unknown. If an allergic reaction occurs, azithromycin should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. Physicians should remain vigilant for the potential recurrence of allergic symptoms after stopping symptomatic treatment. 2. Cases of hepatotoxicity, including abnormal liver function, hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic failure, have been reported with azithromycin use, some of which have resulted in death. Azithromycin should be discontinued immediately if signs or symptoms of hepatitis occur. 3. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including azithromycin, and can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibiotic use disrupts the normal flora of the colon, allowing overgrowth of C. difficile, which produces toxins A and B that contribute to CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile can lead to increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be resistant to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic use, even up to two months after the last dose. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, antibiotic treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be initiated as clinically indicated. 4. Azithromycin, like other macrolides, has been associated with prolonged cardiac repolarization and QT interval, which increases the risk of developing cardiac arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes. Cases of torsades de pointes have been reported during post-marketing surveillance in patients receiving azithromycin. Providers should carefully weigh the risks and benefits of azithromycin in patients at risk for QT prolongation, including those with known QT interval prolongation, a history of torsades de pointes, congenital long QT syndrome, bradyarrhythmias, uncompensated heart failure, or ongoing proarrhythmic conditions such as uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia. Patients on drugs known to prolong the QT interval or receiving Class IA or Class III antiarrhythmic agents should also be considered at risk. Elderly patients may be more susceptible to drug-associated effects on the QT interval. 5. Azithromycin is primarily eliminated via the liver, so caution should be exercised when administering it to patients with impaired hepatic function. Limited data are available for patients with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <10 mL/min, and caution is advised when prescribing azithromycin in this population. Intravenous azithromycin should be reconstituted and diluted as directed and administered as an infusion over no less than 60 minutes. Higher concentrations should be avoided to reduce the risk of infusion site reactions. Exacerbation of myasthenia gravis symptoms and new-onset myasthenic syndrome have been reported in patients receiving azithromycin therapy. 6. Azithromycin should only be prescribed for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections or prophylactic indications to avoid unnecessary use, which increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Patients should be instructed to discontinue azithromycin and contact their physician if any signs of an allergic reaction occur. They should also be counseled to complete the full course of therapy as directed, even if they feel better early in the treatment course, to ensure effectiveness and reduce the risk of bacterial resistance. 7. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves after discontinuation of the antibiotic. However, patients should be advised to contact their physician if they develop watery and bloody stools, with or without stomach cramps and fever, even as late as two months after completing the antibiotic course. 8. Co-administration of azithromycin with nelfinavir has been shown to increase azithromycin serum concentrations. While dose adjustment is not recommended, close monitoring for known side effects of azithromycin, such as liver enzyme abnormalities and hearing impairment, is warranted. Although azithromycin does not appear to affect prothrombin time in healthy individuals, post-marketing reports suggest that it may potentiate the effects of oral anticoagulants. Prothrombin times should be carefully monitored in patients receiving azithromycin and oral anticoagulants concomitantly. 9. Drug interaction studies with azithromycin have shown modest effects on the pharmacokinetics of drugs such as atorvastatin, carbamazepine, cetirizine, didanosine, efavirenz, fluconazole, indinavir, midazolam, rifabutin, sildenafil, theophylline, triazolam, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and zidovudine. No dosage adjustments are recommended when azithromycin is co-administered with these agents. However, careful monitoring is advised when azithromycin is used with digoxin, ergotamine, dihydroergotamine, terfenadine, cyclosporine, hexobarbital, or phenytoin due to potential interactions observed with other macrolides. 10. Long-term animal studies have not been conducted to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of azithromycin. However, standard laboratory tests have shown no evidence of mutagenicity or impaired fertility. 11. Azithromycin is classified as Pregnancy Category B. Animal studies have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Azithromycin should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. 12. It is not known whether azithromycin is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administering azithromycin to nursing women. 13. The safety and effectiveness of azithromycin for injection in children under 16 years of age have not been established. However, azithromycin has been administered orally to pediatric patients aged 6 months to 16 years in controlled clinical studies. 14. Pharmacokinetic studies of intravenous azithromycin in older adults have not been performed, but oral pharmacokinetics in older volunteers (65–85 years) were similar to those in younger adults (18–40 years). Clinical trials of intravenous azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia included a significant proportion of elderly patients, and no overall differences in safety or efficacy were observed compared to younger patients. However, elderly patients may be more susceptible to torsades de pointes arrhythmia.
